A1: Citations are correct, but it says Córdoba et al. 2019 'mostly compares cold brew settings with each other, not cold with hot'. In fact that paper compares cold with hot and finds cold brew has higher pH and lower titratable acidity, making it a valid third study. It also understates the 2020 Foods pH result: cold brew pH was higher at every roast, by 0.20-0.34 units.
A2: All four citations exist with correct authors, year, journal, volume and article number.
A3: Rightly separates pH from titratable acidity, but overcorrects to 'pH about the same', which the 2020 and 2019 papers contradict.
A4: Says it is working from memory and marks the third study as partial.
A5: Hedged appropriately, with no spurious numbers.
A6: Distinguishes the different measures of acidity.
A7: Delivers two direct studies plus one partial, and misjudges the real third one.
A8: Does not say what evidence would change the conclusion.
A9: Gives usable citations and safe wording.

A1: States flatly that Córdoba et al. 2019 'only study cold brew without comparing it to hot brew'. That is false: the paper compares the two and reports lower titratable acidity and higher pH for cold brew, so it is exactly the study the user asked for. Also says 2020 pH differences were 'small as in 2018' and rates the 'not less acidic by pH' inversion HIGH, against the 2020 data.
A2: Citations real and correctly detailed. The 2018 pH range of 4.85-5.13 matches the paper.
A3: Raises the absolutism issue but builds a false counter-premise.
A5: Precise 85-90% / ~75% figures, and HIGH confidence in an inversion that the evidence partly contradicts.
A6: Covers pH vs titratable acidity vs perceived sourness.
A7: Refuses a third study and wrongly dismisses the valid one.
A9: Sends the user searching after mischaracterizing the paper they need.
A10: Framework overhead on a citation request.

F3.why: Both have accurate bibliographic details for Rao & Fuller 2018, Rao/Fuller/Grim 2020 and Fuller & Rao 2017, and both miss that Córdoba 2019 is a direct hot-vs-cold comparison. A hedges that claim and still points the user to the paper, while B states the falsehood flatly and builds a stronger 'pH is the same' conclusion than the literature supports.
checked: Rao & Fuller 2018, Sci Rep 8:16030 'Acidity and Antioxidant Activity of Cold Brew Coffee' -> exists (PMC6207714); pH similar, titratable acidity higher in hot brew
Rao, Fuller & Grim 2020, Foods 9(7):902 -> exists with correct title; cold brew pH higher than hot at every roast (gap 0.20-0.34), titratable acidity lower in cold brew, differences significant
Fuller & Rao 2017, Sci Rep 7:17979 on caffeine and chlorogenic acid in cold brew -> exists (PMC5740146)

Córdoba et al. 2019, Sci Rep 9:8440 -> exists, but it DOES compare cold with hot: 'All cold brew coffee samples had lower TA values than their hot counterparts', and cold brew pH was higher; both answers mischaracterize it, B more absolutely
